title: How Much Cash You Should Keep at Home vs. the Bank
description: Disaster preparedness and the limits of the banking system.
content:
We live in a digital world, but physical cash still has a role. Whether it is for a natural disaster (when card readers go down), a yard sale, or just privacy, keeping some currency on hand is a smart diversification strategy. However, hoarding cash under a mattress is dangerous due to theft, fire, and inflation. This guide outlines the 'Safe' amount of physical cash to hold for emergencies versus the amount you should keep in the bank.

Key Takeaways

  • The 3-Day Rule: FEMA recommends having enough cash to cover small needs for 3 days if power/ATMs are down. ~$200-$500 is usually sufficient.
  • The $1,000 Limit: Most Homeowner/Renter insurance policies limit cash coverage to $200 or $1,000. If your house burns down with $50k inside, you lose $49k. Check your policy.
  • Denominations: Keep small bills ($1s, $5s, $10s). In a power outage scenario, shops cannot make change for a $100 bill.
  • Opportunity Cost: Cash at home earns 0%. Cash in a bank earns 5% (HYSA). Keeping $10,000 at home costs you $500/year in lost interest.

Why It Matters (US Context)

US currency is fiat. It has value because the government says so. In hyper-inflation or societal collapse, cash might be worthless anyway. Do not become a 'Doomsday Prepper' with life savings in a wall. Use cash for local disruptions (hurricanes/ice storms), not the apocalypse.

The Cash Portfolio

Balance access with safety.

1. The 'Wallet' Stash ($100)

Keep $40-$100 in your wallet.
Use: Cash-only taco trucks, tipping, parking garages that don't take cards.

2. The 'Hurricane' Stash ($500 - $1,000)

Keep this in a fireproof safe bolted to the floor.
Use: Buying gas/food during a power outage. Paying a contractor for emergency tree removal.
Format: Small bills.

3. The Bank Stash ($10k+)

Everything else stays here.
Why: FDIC insurance protects it from theft. Interest protects it from inflation.
Access: You can withdraw $500/day from an ATM if needed.

Safety Protocols

  1. Fireproof Box: Mandatory. If you keep >$100 at home, buy a UL-rated fire box. It protects against fire, but a thief can carry it away. Hide it well.
  2. Tell Your Spouse: If you hide money in a book and die, your family might donate the book. Ensure one other person knows the location.
  3. Don't Brag: Never tell friends/neighbors you keep cash at home. It makes you a target.
  4. Rotate It: Old bills can get moldy or damaged. Spend the stash and replenish it with fresh bills from the bank once a year.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is a Safe Deposit Box good?

No. Banks prohibit storing cash in safe deposit boxes. Also, if the bank is closed (emergency), you can't get to it. Keep emergency cash at home.

What about Gold?

Gold coins are a good alternative for larger amounts because they are compact and fireproof. But you can't buy bread with a gold coin easily. Cash is for spending; Gold is for storing.

Does homeowners insurance cover theft?

Yes, but usually only up to $200 for cash. You need a 'rider' for more, and insurers rarely write riders for cash because fraud is too easy.
